previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, chronic steroid use, bilateral corneal transplants, and multiple comorbidities was admitted following sudden onset of right retro-orbital headache and right eye vision changes, including red desaturation and blurriness, after a brief loss of consciousness. Initial evaluation at an eye specialty center prompted transfer for further neurological assessment. Imaging including CT head, MRI brain and orbits, and MRA of head and neck showed no acute intracranial abnormality, mass, or vascular dissection. Laboratory studies were stable, with normal renal function and potassium. The clinical picture was most consistent with right optic neuritis, likely related to his underlying autoimmune condition. Pain was managed conservatively, and no changes were made to his chronic medications, including dexamethasone and azathioprine. He was discharged home with instructions to follow up with neurology and ophthalmology, to start outpatient terbinafine for a fungal infection, and to monitor for worsening symptoms. Pending blood tests include fungal cultures, RPR, and ACE levels.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___, 

 You were admitted to the ___ 
after you had audiovisual hallucinations and were found to be 
hypotensive and have acute renal failure. These symptoms were 
consistent with an adrenal crisis, which is caused by an 
insufficient production of hormones by your adrenal glands, 
usually in the setting of some sort of stress. 

 You were given hydrocortisone and intravenous fluids in the 
emergency department and your home carvedilol was stopped. Your 
blood pressure gradually returned to normal levels. By the time 
of your discharge, your pressures had returned your baseline 
range, and we restarted your home carvedilol.  

 At this time, there is no clear event that caused this adrenal 
crisis. It is possible the symptoms represent an adverse 
reaction to the rituximab you received the day prior to the 
onset of your symptoms. Other possible causes include 
infections, but you had no symptoms of infection in the days 
before your admission. A chest x-ray showed no signs of 
pneumonia and blood cultures have shown no evidence of infection 
to date. Analysis of your urine did not find evidence of an 
infection. 

We have made one change to your home medications.
1. STOP ___

We discontinued this medication because it can contribute to 
hallucinations, and can also worsen changes in blood pressure 
with standing. You should speak with your primary care physician 
before starting ___ again. 

It was a pleasure to participate in your care at ___.
